The Prime Wavelet Tree

Compressing the Carmichael Numbers

Ankur Gupta, Jonathan Webster and Sylvia Webster
Butler University

arXiv:2610.02550. Submitted to DCC 2027.

A. Shallue and J. Webster computed all 308,279,939 Carmichael numbers below 1024 with their prime factors. Their table takes 18.4 GB as text. Our smallest file stores the numbers in 588.7 MB, or 15.28 bits per number, which is 31.2 times smaller than the text. It recovers the whole table, every prime factor included, in 11 minutes on one core. This site gives the code, the data files and the measurements behind the paper.

Results

Three on/off switches define the eight cells. Switch A stores the divisor dmin(n), from which n follows, instead of n. Switch B stores each prime set as a path in a prime wavelet tree (PWT) instead of storing numbers in a sorted list. Switch C codes the values with residue classes or entropy coding instead of one byte-aligned VByte code each. Each cell has a page with its file, hash, times and commands.

The eight cells and the d∗ row, on all 308,279,939 Carmichael numbers (CNs) below 1024.

Space is the file size in bits per CN: bytes × 8 / 308,279,939.

Times are single-threaded minutes on an Intel Core i9-9900K (8 cores, 16 threads), 64 GB RAM, NVMe SSD, Windows 10, unless noted. Build runs from the oracle to the finished file. Decode times are in memory and exclude loading the file (2 to 10 seconds). The lists of n decode in sorted order. Sorting the output of the others takes 0.8 minutes more.

Decoding CNs + primes adds the time to factor what the cell does not store. Factoring times are single-thread costs per number, measured on every 100th block of 4,096 CNs (3,084,288 CNs in all) and scaled to all CNs. Every factorization of the full table was also checked against the oracle.

†The dmin list itself decodes in 0.03 min (cell 100) and 0.61 min (cell 101). The rest is factoring every dmin.

‡The divisors d∗ are chosen by a heuristic search in place of dmin (cell 111x).

§This is the wall-clock time as run, not on one thread. It took 18.6 min for the dmin paths on 15 threads, 33.1 h for the divisor search (five sweeps) on 6 threads and 7.5 min for encoding on 4 threads. The file stores the chosen divisors, so it can be rebuilt without repeating the search, in about 13 minutes.

Bold marks the best value of each measure, and the darker cells the smallest file. In the last column, download leads to a hosted file and rebuild to the commands that rebuild a file from the oracle.

Quick start

Clone the repository and run the commands below. The code is C++20 with no external libraries.

git clone https://github.com/ankurgupta-cs/prime-wavelet-tree.git
cd prime-wavelet-tree
make check                      # self-test, no download
make fetch-111x verify-111x     # download the smallest file and check it
make fetch-oracle certify-111x  # compare every CN with the oracle
make rebuild-011                # rebuild cell 011 from the oracle (12.7 min)

The reproduce page gives the time, download, memory and disk of each step.
